title: Practical ABAP: values, expressions, and failure paths
intro: Use these worked scenarios after the basic language questions. They test the consequences of parameter passing, aliasing, partial updates, and failure handling rather than syntax recall alone. Modern additions require a supporting target release and language version; examples are teaching scenarios, not executed SAP evidence.

sources.title: SAP: Sharing between dynamic data objects
SAP: LOOP AT itab, GROUP BY

questions.question: What changes when a method receives a CHANGING parameter by value instead of by reference?
questions.answer: By reference, the formal parameter aliases the caller's data, so allowed writes affect it immediately. With VALUE, a local value is changed and copied back on normal completion. An exception leaving the method prevents that normal copy-back. This difference affects error guarantees, but it does not undo database writes or changes made through referenced objects.
questions.detail: Suppose a method changes a plain integer from 10 to 20 and then raises a class-based exception. A reference CHANGING parameter can leave 20 visible to the caller; a value-result parameter retains the caller's 10. Test both failure and success paths before changing an established signature.
questions.pitfall: Pass-by-value is not a transaction rollback and does not clone objects behind reference parameters.
followups: How would this change with an object reference parameter?
Can an IMPORTING reference variable still expose a mutable object?
signals: Separates parameter direction from transfer mode
questions.evidence: A small method-call test showing caller values after normal return and exception.

references.title: SAP: Pass by value
references.note: Formal parameters are local copies; parameter direction controls transfer.

questions.question: A copied structure contains a string, a nested table, and an object reference. Is it an independent snapshot?
questions.answer: The string and nested table are value components: changing their copied contents does not intentionally mutate the source value. The reference component is different: copying it preserves a reference to the same object. Mutating that object's state through either structure is observable through the other. A true snapshot therefore needs an explicit policy for references and mutable reachable objects.
questions.detail: For an approval snapshot, copying ls_request preserves the item values but does not freeze an attached mutable pricing object. Store the calculated price as a value, use an immutable collaborator, or implement deliberate cloning with defined identity and cycle handling. Internal sharing optimizations do not change these language-level semantics.
questions.pitfall: A deep ABAP type is not a promise that ordinary assignment recursively clones the entire object graph.
followups: Which components need copying for an audit snapshot?
How would you test sharing without inspecting memory addresses?
questions.evidence: Mutation tests for a copied string, nested row, and referenced object's attribute.

references.title: SAP: Sharing between dynamic data objects
references.note: Distinguishes copying reference values from internal sharing of strings and tables.

questions.question: A large temporary internal table is no longer needed. When would you choose CLEAR or FREE?
questions.answer: For a headerless internal table, both remove its rows. CLEAR keeps the initial memory requirement available, while FREE also releases that initial allocation. I use CLEAR when the same table will soon be populated again and FREE when retaining its allocation has no useful purpose. Neither deletes the declared variable or guarantees an immediate reduction in operating-system memory.
questions.detail: In a package loop, repeatedly freeing and rebuilding a modest buffer may add allocation work. After a one-off large reconciliation, releasing the unused table can reduce retained application memory. Measure used and allocated memory in the relevant session before drawing conclusions from process memory alone.
questions.pitfall: Do not claim CLEAR retains every byte ever allocated, or that FREE destroys referenced objects still reachable elsewhere.
followups: What changes for an obsolete table with a header line?
Which memory measurement would verify the effect?
signals: Distinguishes row data from initial allocation
questions.evidence: Debugger memory snapshots before population, CLEAR, and FREE.

references.title: SAP: CLEAR
references.note: CLEAR releases table rows but retains the initial memory requirement; FREE releases that too.

questions.question: A dynamic ASSIGN fails, but IS ASSIGNED is still true. How can the program update the wrong field?
questions.answer: A failed dynamic assignment can leave the field symbol pointing at its previous target. IS ASSIGNED then says only that some assignment exists, not that the latest lookup succeeded. I check the statement's result immediately and avoid using the alias after failure. On a supporting release, ELSE UNASSIGN makes the failure state explicit; otherwise I unassign before attempting the lookup.
questions.detail: A mapper assigns component PRICE successfully, then requests nonexistent component PRCIE. If it tests only IS ASSIGNED, a subsequent write may overwrite PRICE. A regression test must include a successful lookup followed by an invalid one using the same field symbol.
questions.pitfall: An assigned field symbol is not evidence that the most recent dynamic ASSIGN succeeded.
followups: How would you fix this on a release without ELSE UNASSIGN?
Why can a test containing only the invalid name miss the defect?
questions.evidence: A valid-then-invalid component lookup leaves the original component unchanged.

references.title: SAP: ASSIGN, ELSE UNASSIGN
references.note: Failed assignments may preserve an earlier alias unless explicitly unassigned.

questions.question: A READ TABLE fails, yet a later IF sy-subrc = 0 takes the success branch. What do you inspect?
questions.answer: I inspect every intervening statement that can set sy-subrc. It is a shared runtime field, not a result permanently attached to READ TABLE. I branch immediately or preserve the result in a named local variable before further work. For modern expressions, I use their documented exception or predicate behavior instead of assuming they set sy-subrc like classic statements.
questions.detail: A failed lookup is followed by a successful FIND used to prepare logging text. Testing sy-subrc afterward now tests FIND. Include a missing-record case with successful logging preparation; merely testing an immediate lookup in isolation would miss the actual sequence.
questions.pitfall: Not every statement resets sy-subrc, and a table expression is not a drop-in sy-subrc-producing READ TABLE.
followups: Which exact statement last wrote sy-subrc?
Would line_exists plus a second lookup improve this case?
questions.evidence: A regression sequence proves missing input cannot be treated as found after another operation.

references.title: SAP: SY-SUBRC
references.note: Return values belong to particular statements and can be replaced by later statements.

questions.question: An import must reject precision loss rather than silently round or truncate. Where does EXACT help?
questions.answer: EXACT requests a lossless assignment or calculation and raises an appropriate exception when the requested result cannot be represented without loss. CONV applies ordinary conversion rules and is not equivalent validation. I place the check at a typed boundary, translate conversion failures into useful input feedback, and still validate domain rules such as permitted signs, identifiers, and currency.
questions.detail: Converting a runtime text longer than a fixed character target can otherwise discard characters. For a two-decimal packed result, EXACT can reject a calculation such as one divided by three. That is useful when rounding is forbidden; when rounding is required, make the business rounding step explicit instead.
questions.pitfall: EXACT does not prove that a technically representable value is an allowed business value.
followups: Which exception family would you translate at the import boundary?
When would requiring exactness reject a legitimate business calculation?
signals: Separates numeric loss from business validation
questions.evidence: Boundary tests include fitting data, truncation, rounding, and numeric overflow.

references.title: SAP: EXACT examples
references.note: Official executable illustrations of lossless assignments and calculations.

questions.question: Two invoice totals differ by one cent although both use decimal types. How do you diagnose rounding?
questions.answer: I compare the sequence of calculations, intermediate precision, and the prescribed rounding point and mode. Rounding every line and then summing can differ from summing precise values and rounding once. Currency metadata does not automatically make an arbitrary calculation compliant. I retain currency context, use appropriate decimal types, and encode the agreed rule explicitly with boundary tests.
questions.detail: Under an agreed half-up, two-decimal rule, two positive line results of 0.005 become 0.01 each if rounded separately, totaling 0.02. Their unrounded sum is 0.010 and rounds to 0.01. The correct amount depends on the specified line-versus-document rule.
questions.pitfall: Choosing decfloat34 or formatting two decimals does not settle the business rounding policy.
followups: How do negative half-way values affect the selected mode?
Where is currency conversion applied relative to tax rounding?
questions.evidence: Worked positive/negative boundary examples with independently calculated expected totals.

references.title: SAP: Rounding function ROUND
references.note: Decimal places, precision, and explicit rounding modes are distinct choices.

questions.question: Why can replacing MOVE-CORRESPONDING with CORRESPONDING erase an existing structure field?
questions.answer: An ordinary CORRESPONDING constructor creates a new result, so target components absent from the source become initial. MOVE-CORRESPONDING between structures leaves unmatched target components unchanged. BASE can supply starting values for a constructor result before matching components overwrite them. I specify the desired merge contract rather than assuming all name-based assignments preserve existing state.
questions.detail: ls_existing contains status Approved and a note. The source contains only a new note: plain CORRESPONDING clears the unmatched status; BASE preserves it. But if the source type contains status with an initial value, that matching component still overwrites the base. Field presence requires a separate update contract.
questions.pitfall: BASE preserves unmatched components; it does not mean ignore every initial source value or implement PATCH automatically.
followups: What happens when status exists but is initial in the source?
How do table BASE semantics differ from structure merging?
questions.evidence: A three-case test covers absent component, initial matching component, and populated matching component.

references.title: SAP: Working with structures
references.note: Compares MOVE-CORRESPONDING with CORRESPONDING and BASE.

questions.question: Unsorted orders must be processed once per customer with their member rows. How does GROUP BY change the loop?
questions.answer: LOOP AT with GROUP BY first forms groups and then executes the group loop. Equal group keys are collected even if rows are not adjacent, unlike traditional control-level processing that relies on ordering. I choose explicit group-key binding when it improves clarity and use LOOP AT GROUP for members. Group order and member order still need a deliberate contract.
questions.detail: Input customers A, B, A creates two groups, with both A orders together. The group body executes twice, not once per order. WITHOUT MEMBERS is suitable when only group keys are needed, but then a later member loop is not available.
questions.pitfall: Grouping an internal table is not database aggregation, and its default group order is not automatically business sort order.
followups: When would you aggregate at the database instead?
Why must a representative row not be mistaken for a group total?
questions.evidence: An A/B/A fixture proves group membership, counts, and explicit ordering.

references.title: SAP: LOOP AT itab, GROUP BY
references.note: Grouping and group iteration are separate phases; prior sorting is not required.

questions.question: A FILTER expression is proposed for a standard table with an empty primary key. Is that enough?
questions.answer: For the basic FILTER form, access must use a suitable sorted or hashed key. A standard table can work when it has an appropriate secondary key selected with USING KEY; an empty primary key alone is insufficient. I also check that the predicate meets the selected key's rules. A FOR expression or a clear loop may fit an arbitrary predicate better.
questions.detail: A standard table retains arrival order but has a sorted secondary key by customer. FILTER USING KEY can select that customer. A complex OR predicate over unrelated columns should not be forced into a key-based FILTER shape or justified by an unmeasured speed claim.
questions.pitfall: FILTER is not a general-purpose synonym for every WHERE expression supported by LOOP or FOR.
followups: What must a hashed-key predicate provide?
Would adding a secondary key be worthwhile for a single filtering pass?
questions.evidence: Target-release syntax check plus equivalence tests against an explicit loop.

references.title: SAP: FILTER, basic form
references.note: Defines sorted/hash key requirements and supported predicate forms.

questions.question: A REDUCE expression calculates a maximum, but all-negative input returns zero. What went wrong?
questions.answer: The accumulator's initial value is part of the algorithm. Starting a maximum at zero invents a candidate that may not exist in an all-negative input set. I define empty-input semantics and initialize from a valid first member or represent the absence of a result explicitly. I also choose accumulator types deliberately so intermediate overflow or rounding cannot hide behind concise syntax.
questions.detail: For values -8 and -3, a zero-initialized maximum remains zero although the correct maximum is -3. Empty input may require no result or a domain exception, not the same number. The expression should remain readable enough that reviewers can identify initialization, iteration, and state update.
questions.pitfall: REDUCE does not supply mathematically correct initial values or empty-set semantics on the developer's behalf.
followups: How would you represent maximum of an empty set?
Can a narrow accumulator overflow before assignment to a wider result?
questions.evidence: Tests cover empty, one row, all-negative values, mixed signs, and overflow limits.

references.title: SAP: Table reductions, structured result
references.note: Shows explicit initialization and iterative accumulator updates.

questions.question: A report accepts a filter value and a sort-column name. Is escaping quotes sufficient for safe SQL?
questions.answer: No. Data values and SQL identifiers are different inputs. I bind values through host variables in static ABAP SQL where possible. For configurable identifiers or dynamic clauses, I restrict them to a server-controlled allowlist and validate the supported syntax. Escaping a string value cannot authorize a table name, column name, operator, or an entire user-supplied WHERE fragment.
questions.detail: A search value containing an apostrophe should remain a value. A sort request is mapped from an accepted business option to a known column; arbitrary SQL text is rejected. Authorization predicates are built independently and cannot be removed by user filter or ordering choices.
questions.pitfall: Input that is safely quoted as a literal is not therefore safe as SQL syntax or an authorized data access.
followups: How would you test an input that is valid syntax but unauthorized?
Which parts of the SQL shape can remain completely static?
questions.evidence: Negative tests for quoted values, forbidden columns, injected operators, and unauthorized records.

references.title: SAP: Prevent SQL injection
references.note: Prefer static SQL; validate and escape dynamic content using supported facilities.

questions.question: A resource release is placed only in CLEANUP. Why can it remain unreleased after success?
questions.answer: ABAP CLEANUP is part of exception unwinding, not a finally block that runs after every TRY. It runs for the relevant protected context when an exception propagates to an outer handler; it is not the normal-success path. I arrange explicit release on successful completion and on relevant exceptional exits, while respecting the actual owner's lock or resource lifetime.
questions.detail: An application-owned temporary handle is opened, processing succeeds, and ENDTRY is reached: CLEANUP alone does not close it. Test success, an exception caught locally, and one propagated outward. Cleanup failures also need handling so they do not obscure the original failure or escape a CLEANUP block.
questions.pitfall: Do not assume CLEANUP automatically runs after a CATCH in the same TRY, or release framework-owned locks prematurely.
followups: What changes when the exception is caught inside the same TRY?
Who owns release when a caller supplied the resource?
questions.evidence: Instrumented resource tests show one correct release on every intended exit.

references.title: SAP: Exception system response
references.note: Explains stack unwinding and when CLEANUP blocks run or do not run.

questions.question: An optional limit parameter is omitted in one call and explicitly set to zero in another. How can a method distinguish them?
questions.answer: IS SUPPLIED tests whether an actual parameter was provided, independently of its value. IS INITIAL tests the value and cannot distinguish an omitted zero-defaulted argument from an explicit zero. I use presence only when the API deliberately assigns different meaning to omission. If a wrapper always forwards a parameter, it must preserve the intended presence contract explicitly.
questions.detail: For a pagination helper, omission may mean use the configured limit, while zero may mean return no rows. A wrapper that forwards its own initial variable makes the downstream parameter supplied. Test the direct calls and the wrapper path, rather than silently changing zero into the default.
questions.pitfall: OPTIONAL does not automatically preserve absent-versus-present semantics across another method boundary.
followups: What happens when a wrapper always forwards an optional argument?
Would an explicit request structure with a presence flag be clearer?
questions.evidence: Calls with omitted, explicit zero, and positive limit produce their documented outcomes.

references.title: SAP: IS SUPPLIED
references.note: Presence of an actual argument is independent of its initial value.

questions.question: A single-line INSERT INTO TABLE hits an existing unique primary key. Does it update the existing row?
questions.answer: No. For this internal-table insertion case, the new line is not inserted and sy-subrc indicates the duplicate. The existing row is not an implicit update target. I decide whether the operation means reject, merge, or replace, then implement that policy explicitly. I do not generalize this return-code behavior to every constructor, secondary-key conflict, or database insertion form.
questions.detail: An import contains order 7 twice with different amounts. A unique hashed table prevents duplicate keys, but silently ignoring the second line can conceal inconsistent source data. Compare payloads if duplicates are allowed only when identical; otherwise report both the key and conflicting input position.
questions.pitfall: Uniqueness enforcement is not a complete deduplication policy, and INSERT is not an automatic upsert.
followups: What should happen for identical versus conflicting duplicates?
Why must constructor-expression and secondary-key failures be checked separately?
questions.evidence: Tests distinguish new keys, identical duplicates, and conflicting duplicates without changing the original row accidentally.

references.title: SAP: Populating internal tables
references.note: Single-line insertion with duplicate unique primary key returns sy-subrc 4.

questions.question: An authorization helper returns an empty range table. Why is WHERE field IN range unsafe as the only access restriction?
questions.answer: An initial selection range represents no restriction for IN, so it must not be used to encode 'the user may see nothing.' I define empty authorization results separately and return no rows or reject the operation before querying. Nonempty ranges combine inclusion and exclusion rules; their semantics differ from a plain list whose empty membership set would match nothing.
questions.detail: If a user has no permitted plants, the application must not execute an otherwise unrestricted read with an empty plant range. Keep optional user filters separate from mandatory authorization constraints. Test no permissions as well as one permitted plant and exclusions.
questions.pitfall: An empty ABAP selection range is not the same as an SQL list containing zero allowed values.
followups: How do you distinguish an optional filter from mandatory authorization?
What result do you expect from a range containing only exclusions?
questions.evidence: A denied-user test proves zero data and zero aggregate leakage with an empty authorization result.

references.title: SAP: Comparison with selection tables
references.note: Defines inclusion/exclusion semantics and the initial selection-table case.
